Our community exists everywhere. The queer community is a global community, and it’s wonderful to remember that. Even at the darkest times, we have a community to turn to. I can’t take any responsibility, but it feels like a Christmas miracle to not have to be fighting as hard to get people to listen to something that should be basic information.

BENDELACRÈME: Every year, we try to create a show that speaks to where we’re at collectively. But this year’s show is about how the future is always unknown. It’s always scary, and it’s always true that nothing is inevitable. We’ve been fed a lot of rhetoric about inevitable futures, and the next thing can be anything. And so, to write a show with that content and then get to open it riding this wave of hope — but also remembering that the conversations don’t happen by themselves — is very special. We’ve got to keep up with it. We’ve got to stay behind it. It’s very exciting — things coinciding in a way that’s just celebratory and hopeful.

MONSOON: We like to have the serious conversations in the stupidest way possible. With the Christmas/Winter holiday lens, we try to keep it in the world of commonly recognizable fictional Christmas characters, and luckily, there’s a large repertoire to pull from. Scrooge really fits the build this year.

What I love about the show is that we’re having conversations that every artist out there is having: How do I make a living being an artist while staying true to creating art? I also have to feed myself, and this all doesn’t just happen magically for free. It’s the dilemma a lot of artists are facing. Do you want to be an artist or do you want to eat? And for a long time, you haven’t had to decide one or the other. But art has been attacked and left out to fend for itself recently, and everything’s about what’s going to make money, not what’s the best possible art. So I think, as a performer, I’m very excited to be a live entertainer because, for whatever reason, art is surviving and thriving in live entertainment — even though a lot of filmed media feels like it’s being pushed through the same sausage maker of capitalism.

DELA: Fortunately, for now, live entertainment — seeing a performer in front of you — is one of the few things we can still really trust is real and happening, right? It’s very scary, but I think we’re also all really learning to be skeptical in a way that’s really important. It’s also really hard to approach everything with a sense of, “Can I believe this?” But when you’re in a room with someone, you know it’s real. It’s in front of your eyes, but you can also feel it, right? You don’t exchange energy with people over a screen in the same way. You don’t. People can feel each other’s presence, and they can feel what it means. I think that’s part of why live performance continues to thrive and will continue to thrive.

MONSOON: Every year we come to our first writing session like a completely blank slate. Usually, Dela has a couple of assignments — maybe there’s a top 40 song, or there’s a cultural moment or there was a movie — and she says, “We are doing a disservice to our audience if we don’t get a bit in about this thing.” This year, we lost two huge multigenerational queer icons who are very much alive in the zeitgeist and still are.

Dela just came to the table saying, “I don’t know how we’re going to do it, but we got to get a Dolly song, and we got to get a Tim Curry song, and I think I know which Tim Curry song. We’ve just got to find the right way.” And the way she found to incorporate it is so perfectly suited to the taste of “The Jinkx and Dela Holiday Show.” It’s so perfect. It’s nothing you would have imagined outside of the context of “The Jinkx and Dela Holiday Show,” but within the show, it’s a seat of honor.

#734. Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years

A chemistry challenge that had frustrated researchers for more than 60 years has finally been overcome. Scientists at the University of Würzburg in Germany have discovered a way to produce and isolate oxoboranes, a group of unusual molecules that were long considered too unstable to study under ordinary laboratory conditions.

The breakthrough, published in Nature Chemistry, was led by Professor Holger Braunschweig and his team, with computational support from researchers led by Professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India. Their findings reveal a surprisingly straightforward way to create these elusive compounds, potentially opening new possibilities for molecular chemistry.

Boron is an element that rarely forms triple bonds, a type of chemical connection in which two atoms share three pairs of electrons. For more than 15 years, Braunschweig has focused on overcoming this limitation and creating molecules containing unusual bonds involving boron.

His laboratory has already achieved several important milestones. In 2012, the team reported the first molecule containing a triple bond between two boron atoms. Another breakthrough followed in 2025, when the researchers produced the first neutral molecule featuring a triple bond between boron and carbon.

One major challenge remained among the elements in the first row of the periodic table's p-block. Researchers had yet to isolate stable organic oxoboranes, molecules characterized by a triple bond between boron and oxygen.

Chemists around the world had been pursuing these compounds since at least the early 1960s. Over the decades, scientists working in both organic and inorganic chemistry had managed to detect and trap oxoboranes under extreme conditions. Other experiments provided indirect evidence of their existence, and researchers succeeded in creating several related derivatives. However, obtaining stable examples that could be isolated and examined remained an unsolved problem.

An Unexpected Reaction Produces Elusive Molecules

The long-awaited breakthrough emerged from experiments that initially appeared to be heading in a different direction.

Two doctoral students at the University of Würzburg, Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl, were independently investigating reactions between a compound known as a diboracumulene and various ketones, which are commonly used chemicals in organic synthesis.

Both researchers noticed something unusual. Instead of producing only the outcomes they might have expected, the reactions generated distinctive orange or yellow solids.

"The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something," says Lukas Lubczyk.

What made the results particularly remarkable was that oxoboranes emerged as the main products of these reactions, even though several other chemical outcomes had appeared more likely. After decades of unsuccessful efforts to isolate such molecules, the researchers had found that they could form unexpectedly from reactions involving relatively simple starting materials.

Braunschweig described just how surprising the discovery was to scientists familiar with the long-standing challenge.

"Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them," says Holger Braunschweig.

Using their newly discovered method, the scientists successfully prepared three different oxoboranes. The fact that the approach worked with multiple compounds suggests that it could provide access to a much wider range of these previously difficult to isolate molecules.

The team is now investigating how broadly the technique can be applied. Beyond producing additional oxoboranes, the researchers hope to determine whether similar strategies could help them create other elusive compounds involving elements throughout the periodic table.

The discovery not only resolves a problem that challenged chemists for more than six decades but also demonstrates how unexpected chemical reactions can reveal possibilities that researchers once considered beyond reach.

International Research Collaboration and Funding

The findings were published through a collaboration between the Würzburg research team and the group led by Professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University (India), whose computational research helped support the work.

Funding was provided by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier.

The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable.

The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase.

Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher, Google's planned AI constellation).

The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short. The goal was to "demonstrate technologies necessary for future debris-removal missions as well as for future applications in the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft," according to NASA's SSPICY site.

"This advances NASA's in-space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) goals to ensure a sustainable space operating environment and builds towards a future where objects can be assembled, repaired and maintained in space, significantly expanding possibilities for science and human exploration," the agency added.

Starfish Space was a natural partner. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing, using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers.

SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections.

But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous.

"While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post.

"An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable."

The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain.

"The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said.

Otter Pup 2 is now operating as close as 25 meters away from @GilmourSpace's ElaraSat, fully autonomously. This vid contains imagery captured when we were separated by just 33.6 meters. We’ve demonstrated our ability to safely and precisely operate at very close range, executing intricate maneuvers, gathering detailed imagery, and testing the capabilities we’ll need for docking. With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history.October 27, 2026

The Seattle company has other work to do in LEO at the moment as well: Its Otter Pup 2 prototype craft is currently gearing up to conduct a historic docking of its own in LEO.

Otter Pup 2, which launched in June 2025, has been getting closer and closer to another private spacecraft, Gilmour Space's ElaraSat. Last week, the company announced that Otter Pup 2 got within a mere 82 feet (25 meters) of its target.

"With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history," Starfish Space said in an Oct. 27 X post.

Two private satellites have docked before, but only much higher above Earth, in geostationary orbit. Such a meetup has not yet happened in LEO.

#732. Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE)

Sylvester Stallone wrote “Rocky” in three days. Figuring out which Oscar screenplay category the movie about him writing it belongs in is taking a lot longer.

Amazon MGM Studios’ “I Play Rocky” has been the subject of multiple conversations among the studio, the Writers Guild of America, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and the film’s creative team over whether Peter Gamble’s script will compete as an original or adapted screenplay. No determination has been made. Related Stories Dear Oscars: Don’t Let Laika and ‘Wildwood’ Fail. There Is No Backup Stop-Motion Studio Waiting in the Wings 'The Odyssey' Oscar Blitz to Begin With Robert Downey Jr., Guillermo del Toro and Steven Spielberg as Moderators

Thursday, Nov. 12, is the final deadline for studios to submit Official Screen Credits (OSC) forms to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for the 99th Academy Awards in the best picture, animated feature and general entry categories. No films afterward will be considered.

Gamble conceived and wrote the script as an original, and it isn’t based on a book, article, memoir or any other single published work. He drafted it on spec, and Bellevue Productions, shared it with Christian Baha of Baha Films. Baha came aboard as a producer alongside Toby Emmerich, and director Peter Farrelly, who helmed best picture winner “Green Book” (2018), eventually signed on. It’s Gamble’s second produced feature script after “Office Uprising” (2018).

But “Rocky” is one of the most established pieces of IP in Hollywood, and sources say some within each organization are weighing whether the screenplay is a better fit for adapted, the category for scripts built on previously established material. Rocky Balboa, Adrian and Apollo Creed are preexisting characters and Farrelly’s film restages some of the 1976 movie’s best-known scenes, written half a century ago.

Amazon MGM and the Academy declined to comment.

“I Play Rocky” expands nationwide Nov. 20, the same day WGA submissions close, but the guild won’t be weighing in. The film wasn’t produced under a WGA signatory agreement, so the guild can’t classify the screenplay or consider it for the WGA Awards, even though Gamble is a member. That leaves the decision entirely to the Academy’s Writers Branch executive committee, which makes its own determinations and has broken with the WGA before.

Elsewhere on the circuit, the question will carry less weight. The Golden Globes put all screenplays in a single category, while BAFTA and the Critics Choice Awards, which split original and adapted, generally go with the category the studio submits.

According to the Academy’s screenplay submission FAQ for the 99th Oscars, films don’t submit to a specific writing category. Instead, the Writers Branch executive committee reviews each eligible title and generally defers to the WGA’s classification, except when the guild hasn’t classified a film, as is the case with “I Play Rocky” or its classification “has been called into question.” The guidelines cut both ways for Gamble’s script.

A script is generally deemed adapted if it’s based on a sequel, a remake, an existing film or “pre-existing characters,” but it’s considered original if it tells a true story in which the writer “performed their own research and used multiple sources.” While a determination is under review, the committee may ask the film’s credited writers for a statement. Once it rules, the decision is final and no appeals or additional materials are accepted.

We seem to have one of these every awards season.

In January 2024, Greta Gerwig’s “Barbie” was moved to adapted after Warner Bros. campaigned it as an original and the WGA classified as well. Barbie and Ken existed as Mattel dolls long before Gerwig and Noah Baumbach turned them into a billion-dollar sensation, and there were multiple cartoons that existed with the characters. Ultimately, the script earned an adapted nomination and lost to Cord Jefferson’s “American Fiction.”

Category reversals aren’t new. Barry Jenkins’ “Moonlight,” Damien Chazelle’s “Whiplash” and Joel and Ethan Coen’s “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs” all carried original labels from the WGA before the Academy shifted them to adapted. The Academy has also long treated sequels as adaptations because their characters come from earlier films, which is how “Before Sunset,” “Toy Story 3,” “Top Gun: Maverick” and “Glass Onion” all landed in adapted.

That rule is being tested again this season. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” which dramatizes whistleblower Frances Haugen’s 2021 Facebook leak and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz’s coverage of it, was initially marketed as a sequel to “The Social Network” (2010), which won Sorkin the adapted screenplay Oscar. The WGA has classified the new film as an original. There’s no word yet on whether the Academy’s committee will accept that designation.

That’s the precedent Gamble’s script has to get around, and there’s a strong counterargument. “I Play Rocky” isn’t a sequel, a prequel or a spinoff. It’s a biographical drama about a real person, and biopics have routinely competed as originals. Dustin Lance Black won original screenplay for “Milk,” even though Harvey Milk’s life had already been chronicled in the Oscar-winning documentary “The Times of Harvey Milk.” Anthony McCarten’s “Darkest Hour” also competed as an original, despite covering Winston Churchill’s first weeks as prime minister, a chapter that fills every high school history textbook.

Movies about the making of movies are interesting territory, and they have produced originals, too. “Saving Mr. Banks,” about the making of “Mary Poppins,” competed as an original but didn’t land a nomination. Neither did Jason Reitman and Gil Kenan’s “Saturday Night,” which follows the 90 minutes leading up to the first televised episode of “Saturday Night Live.” Netflix’s “Mank,” written by the late Jack Fincher, father of director David Fincher, chronicles screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz’s work on Orson Welles’ “Citizen Kane” (1941). It was also deemed an original, and it also missed in the category, even as the film led the field with 10 nominations.

When a making-of film does land in adapted, there’s usually a book behind it. Scott Neustadter and Michael H. Weber’s “The Disaster Artist,” for example, was based on Greg Sestero and Tom Bissell’s 2013 nonfiction book of the same name. A public figure’s life, however, is fair game, as illustrated by A24’s Chris Hansen story, “Primetime,” which Ajon Singh based on an article by Luke Dittrich.

Interestingly, Amazon MGM owns the “Rocky” franchise. The 1976 original earned 10 Oscar nominations and won best picture, and Stallone was nominated for best actor and original screenplay. Director Farrelly knows the original side all too well, as he shared the original screenplay Oscar with Brian Hayes Currie and Nick Vallelonga for “Green Book,” another true story that drew from no single published source.

Where the film lands could reshape its trajectory, and both races are stacked. In original, Jesse Eisenberg (“The Debut”), Jordan Firstman (“Club Kid”), Mike Leigh (“Tender Loving Care”), Martin McDonagh (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Simon Rich (“Artificial”) are all in the conversation. A move to adapted wouldn’t clear the road. It would put Gamble up against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Drew Goddard’s “Project Hail Mary” and Rashida Jones and Will McCormack’s “The Invite,” along with Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and Denis Villeneuve’s yet-to-be-screened “Dune: Part Three.”

“I Play Rocky” has been gaining momentum since its world premiere at TIFF. It finished first runner-up for the People’s Choice Award behind “La Bola Negra” and was the runner-up at Middleburg. It was also the audience choice winner at Cinéfest Sudbury International Film Festival, and recently Ippolito was honored with the breakthrough award at SCAD Savannah Film Festival. It recently opened on Nov. 6 in seven theaters, capturing $345,000 from seven theaters, averaging $49,200 per location. The film has also made one category call already: it’s submitted at the Golden Globes as a musical or comedy, joining a field that includes “Wild Horse Nine,” “The Debut” and Amazon MGM stablemate “Project Hail Mary.”

The Academy’s final word likely won’t surface until nominations voting opens Jan. 11, 2027. Before that, the WGA announces its screenplay nominees Jan. 8. Oscar nominations will be announced Jan. 21, and the 99th Oscars take place March 14.

#730. Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining

Researchers have developed a surprisingly simple way to separate crude oil without heating it, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industrial processes. The breakthrough uses an inexpensive membrane that could significantly reduce the energy required for oil refining while lowering operating costs and carbon emissions.

The international research effort was led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, in collaboration with Professor Ryan Lively's research group at Georgia Tech. KAIST(President Kwang Hyung Lee) announced that the team had successfully demonstrated a membrane capable of separating crude oil at room temperature. The findings were published in Nature, one of the world's leading scientific journals.

Crude oil is essential for far more than gasoline and other transportation fuels. It also supplies the raw materials used to manufacture plastics, packaging, clothing, and numerous everyday products. Because refining costs affect the prices of these materials, making the process more efficient could have widespread economic and environmental benefits.

Why Traditional Crude Oil Refining Requires So Much Energy

For more than a century, oil refineries have relied heavily on distillation to separate crude oil into useful components. The process involves heating oil to temperatures above 350 °C, turning portions of it into vapor, and then cooling those vapors to collect different fractions.

This approach requires an enormous amount of energy. Worldwide, crude oil distillation consumes approximately 1,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) annually. That is comparable to the combined yearly electricity production of roughly 130 continuously operating nuclear power plants, each with a capacity of about one gigawatt.

The massive energy demand makes distillation a major contributor to both fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions within the refining industry. Meanwhile, growing economic pressures across global petrochemical markets have increased interest in technologies that can separate oil more efficiently.

Membranes have emerged as a promising alternative because they can separate substances without requiring the extreme temperatures used in conventional distillation. However, previous designs have faced significant obstacles.

Traditionally, researchers have assumed that effective molecular separation requires a membrane covered with an extremely thin, specialized coating. Although these coatings can provide the necessary precision, they are expensive to produce and can develop defects when manufactured on a large scale. These limitations have made widespread industrial adoption difficult.

A Surprising Discovery Turns Clogged Filters Into an Advantage

The KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers approached the problem differently. Rather than adding a complicated coating, they used a bare membrane made from porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN), an inexpensive, chemically stable polymer already commonly used as a supporting material in industrial filtration systems.

What happened when crude oil passed through the membrane was unexpected.

As the oil flowed through its pores, heavier hydrocarbon molecules accumulated along the inner walls. This buildup gradually reduced the size of the openings, producing extremely narrow channels measuring less than 2 nanometers across.

In effect, the crude oil helped create the microscopic pathways needed to separate its own components.

These naturally formed channels allowed lighter oil fractions, including naphtha, gasoline, and kerosene, to pass through quickly while preventing heavier substances from traveling through the membrane as easily.

The discovery was especially surprising because the buildup of material inside membrane pores, known as fouling, is normally considered a serious problem. Fouling typically reduces filtration performance and requires cleaning or replacement. In this case, however, the same phenomenon made the membrane highly effective at separating different molecules.

The results were impressive. The uncoated PAN membrane achieved crude oil permeation rates approximately 23 times higher than those reported for previous leading crude oil separation membranes. It also continued operating with stable performance for 28 consecutive days.

Professor Ryan Lively (Georgia Tech) commented: "One of the key challenges facing membrane systems for crude oil separation was the low productivities of the membrane units -- the PAN membranes with their surprising separation mechanism -- dramatically increase the productivity of the membrane unit, to the point where industry should seriously consider adopting the technology."

New Membrane Could Cut Oil Refining Energy Use by Nearly a Third

One of the technology's biggest advantages is that refineries would not necessarily need to replace their existing equipment to use it.

The membrane could instead be installed as a modular filtration system that processes crude oil before it enters conventional distillation equipment. This would reduce the amount of work required during the heating and separation stages while allowing facilities to continue using much of their current infrastructure.

Computer simulations suggest that incorporating the membrane into the refining process could deliver substantial improvements. Energy consumption could fall by 31.6%, while carbon dioxide emissions could decrease by 37.6%. The same calculations projected a 20.7% reduction in cooling water consumption and a 36% decrease in operating costs.

The potential environmental benefits could be considerable if the technology were adopted widely.

Researchers estimate that implementing the system throughout Korea's refining and petrochemical industries could prevent approximately 10 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions each year. That is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions produced by four million vehicles powered by internal combustion engines.

These savings are projections based on process simulations rather than reductions already demonstrated across operating refineries. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that membrane filtration could become a practical way to improve the efficiency of existing facilities.

Although crude oil separation was the main focus of the research, the same technology could eventually be useful in several other industries.

One potential application involves treating pyrolysis oil produced when waste plastics are broken down for recycling. The membranes could also help recover solvents used in battery manufacturing, purify pharmaceutical compounds, and improve biofuel production.

The broader opportunity lies in using complex liquid mixtures to help form the tiny filtration channels needed to separate their components. This approach could provide a more affordable and versatile alternative to conventional membranes that require precisely manufactured surface coatings.

Professor Dong-Yeun Koh of KAIST said, "This study reveals a new scientific principle in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels. Working with real crude oil supplied by HD Hyundai Oilbank allowed us to validate the technology under conditions relevant to industrial operation."

The use of actual crude oil was an important part of the research because it allowed the team to examine how the membrane performed with the complicated mixture of hydrocarbons found in industrial feedstocks.

Before the technology can be deployed more widely, the researchers plan to improve membrane production at larger scales and establish its reliability during extended operation.

Professor Jae W. Lee of KAIST, a co-corresponding author of the study, added, "By advancing large-area membrane modularization and long-term operational reliability, we hope to broaden the adoption of membrane-based processes throughout the refining and petrochemical industries."

Dr. Jihoon Choi and Dr. Hyeokjun Seo of KAIST, the study's co-first authors, said, "Our goal is to precisely control this spontaneous pore-constriction phenomenon and develop it into a membrane platform applicable to the entire refining process. We also aim to expand the technology to plastic recycling, biofuel purification, and other sustainable chemical processes that support carbon neutrality."

The research received support from Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT through the Basic Research Program for Outstanding Early-Career Researchers and the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program.

They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation.

It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay.

That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required.

But now we have been blessed with the news, first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords.

"'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement.

The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson

The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson

"Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together."

As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping.

The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," "The Andromeda Evolution," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix.

Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner.

"Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans.

It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams.

In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson.

Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe.

#728. Pokémon card drops and restocks: Best deals from Amazon, Walmart, TCGplayer

Finding Pokémon card stock at market price hasn’t become any easier in 2026. Of course, you can help your odds by knowing where to look.

When shopping for the 30th Celebration collection, the new Delta Reign expansion, or the Ultra Premium Collection, finding actual stock can be tough. That said, by making the most of important go-tos like Amazon’s invitation system, Best Buy’s own store-only listings, and the occasional restocks elsewhere, you can add to your collection without paying inflated prices.

These are the stores we'd keep bookmarked to have the best chance of getting Pokémon TCG’s new releases. Keep in mind that some of the best options for products are through third-party sellers:

Amazon — One of the more convenient places to find sealed Pokémon products, especially Booster Bundles, ETBs, and Booster Display Boxes. In fact, Amazon recently brought back its $59.99 invitation-only 30th Celebration ETB offer. Select ‘Request invite’ on the Amazon-sold listing; an invitation isn't guaranteed, and the price will likely revert to much higher third-party prices once stock runs out.

TCGplayer — One of the first places to check for preorders on brand new releases, single cards, and listings close to market price. The dedicated trading card site’s "market price" estimations are helpful to gauge whether you’re overpaying for a Pokémon TCG product in the modern market.

Walmart — Regularly carries newly released collections and older expansions, with an extensive selection of products from marketplace sellers, usually at lower prices than Amazon. Not only can you find the in-demand Pokémon TCG 30th Celebration Ultra Premium Collection Night Edition for under market price, but Walmart+ members can sometimes receive early access to restocks.

Best Buy — Among the better options for avoiding reseller markup, thanks to its Pokémon listings that are actually priced at MSRP. For instance, its Prismatic Evolutions ETB is listed at $49.99, although this is another example where you need to request an invite and hope to be randomly selected. Meanwhile, other products sold at MSRP are available only in physical stores. Even if you’re not able to visit in-person Best Buy stores, it's worth registering for online stock drops at MSRP whenever that option becomes available.

Gamestop — Carries the latest expansions alongside older Booster Bundles, Elite Trainer Boxes, and single packs, with some surprising deals that can undercut other sellers. Its Delta Reign Booster Bundle is currently listed at $49.99, with Pro members eligible for a reduced $47.49 price. The retailer's store availability tools are particularly useful for finding nearby stock.

Target — Another useful destination for new collections, particularly if nearby stores have inventory available for pickup. As for online, anything at or near MSRP does unfortunately sell out instantly, and anything readily available comes with a massively jacked-up price. Target has also begun experimenting with invitation systems for certain Pokémon products, including the Destined Rivals Three-Booster Blister, priced at $14.99.

Pokémon Center — The go-to for finding market price and initial drops — plus getting exclusive Pokémon Center Elite Trainer Box editions with additional booster packs and promotional cards. Thanks to the massive imbalance between demand and supply, stock runs out within minutes.

The core issue that’s been plaguing the Pokémon TCG for years comes down to overall demand far outstripping supply; almost any product sells out at MSRP instantly. Between demand from collectors, competitive players, and most importantly, resellers (with many using bot accounts), any preorders or stock drops for new and popular expansions can disappear within minutes of being listed.

The Pokémon Company is printing more cards than ever to help combat the problem. It produced 10 billion cards worldwide during its latest financial year, but even that hasn't been enough to satisfy demand.

That said, the higher volumes during the 30th Celebration have at least affected scalpers' profit margins. More have been available, giving resellers less justification to drive prices above market levels. Moving forward, the company will continue to tackle the shortages while increasing production and promising additional reprints. At the same time, retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target have introduced invitation systems and randomized drawings to reduce the impact of scalpers.

With competition still fierce for the most desirable Pokémon Trading Card Game collections, a little preparation can make the difference between paying MSRP and settling for whatever a reseller is asking:

Sign up for invitations and drawings: Register for Amazon and Best Buy invitations whenever available, and check Target and Walmart for new product draws. These don't guarantee a purchase, but they remove some of the pressure of competing against other shoppers during a live restock.

Check local stores: Best Buy, GameStop, Target, and Walmart can all be worth visiting in person. Online stock may have disappeared, but that doesn't automatically mean every physical location has sold out.

Compare prices before buying: Use TCGplayer to establish the market price for whatever you're looking at, then compare it to the original MSRP.

Follow Pokémon restock trackers: Accounts like @PokemonDealsTCG and @pokemondealsuk on X (formerly Twitter) can help flag new drops, especially when the Pokémon Center opens its virtual queue. Plus, turning on notifications could save you from refreshing multiple store pages throughout the day.

Check who is actually selling the product: Amazon and Walmart regularly feature external sellers, so inspect the seller's details, shipping costs, and estimated delivery dates before committing to a purchase. Third-party sellers are fine to use if they’re selling at around market price and if their rating’s strong.

With Black Friday arriving on Nov. 27, there's a good chance that retailers like Amazon, Walmart, GameStop, Best Buy, and Target will have more Pokémon TCG stock available during their holiday sales.

However, there's currently no guarantee that high-demand products like the 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box or Delta Reign collections will get additional inventory. If there is, these will very likely be very limited, invite-only drops — some even at MSRP if you’re lucky.

Instead, keep checking retailer listings throughout November, especially for older expansions like Perfect Order, Chaos Rising, and Pitch Black, which could see more competitive prices during the sales. It’s usually at these types of shopping events that third-party sellers undercut each other to clear old stock. Any discounts will sell out quickly, so be sure to keep Mashable’s Black Friday buyer’s guides bookmarked throughout the event.

Ben Williams is a freelance writer at Mashable, having joined the team in June 2025. With over 10 years experience in gaming, tech, TV, anime, and film, there’s nothing he hasn’t covered. Alongside Ben’s other work at IGN, Radio Times, Eurogamer, UNILAD Tech, and Rock Paper Shotgun, he also has bylines at sites like GamesRadar+, PCGamesN, ScreenSphere, Twinfinite, ScreenRant, GGRecon, and more.

When away from writing, he spends his downtime playing and watching games, films, and shows he loves covering — whether it’s replaying The Last of Us Part 2, catching Pokémon, rewatching Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood, or bingeing Tarantino movies.

#727. Norwegian Oscar Entry ‘Growth of the Soil’ Sells to North America, U.K., Germany, Spain and More

Beta Cinema has closed a raft of major deals on Hans Petter Moland’s epic love story “Growth of the Soil,” Norway’s entry for best international feature film at the 99th Academy Awards. The deals follow the film’s world premiere in Toronto and its European premiere at San Sebastián, where it walked away with two major awards.

The film has sold to Greenwich Entertainment in North America, Neue Visionen in Germany and Austria, Teodora Film in Italy, A Contracorriente Films in Spain, Conic in the U.K. and Ireland, Cherry Pickers in Benelux, Frenetic Films in Switzerland, Weird Wave in Greece, Scanorama in the Baltics, Vertigo Media in Hungary, Beta Film in Bulgaria, Big Tree Entertainment in India, Falcon Pictures in Indonesia, Imovision in Brazil and Palace Films in Australia and New Zealand. Related Stories Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE) 'I Swear' Star Robert Aramayo on the BAFTA N-Word Incident That Overshadowed the Movie and the ‘X-Men’ Wolverine Pitch He Keeps Hearing

The film was released throughout Scandinavia by Scanbox Entertainment, and got off to a strong start in Norway, climbing to No. 1 at the box office over its opening weekend.

At San Sebastián, “Growth of the Soil” won the Silver Shell for best leading performance and the jury prize for best cinematography. The film has subsequently continued its autumn festival run, including showings at the Warsaw Film Festival, the Rio Film Festival, the Denver Film Festival, the Mar del Plata Film Festival and it opened the Bergen Film Festival. It also is shortlisted for the European Film Awards for the best feature film category.

Based on a Nobel Prize Winning novel, “Growth of the Soil” tells the story of Isak, a man without a past who crosses the mountains in search of somewhere to build a life. High above the tree line, he finds an unforgiving stretch of land and, eventually, Inger, a woman whose resilience matches his own. Together they create a home and family from almost nothing, until time, ambition and a changing world begin to transform both their relationship and the landscape around them.

Herbert Nordrum (“The Worst Person in the World,” “Sense and Sensibility”) and former EFP Shooting Star Asta Kamma August (“The Hypnosis”) are in the leading roles, next to Gard B. Eidsvold, Anders Baasmo, Oddgeir Thune and Sjur Vatne Brean.

Moland previously directed “Out Stealing Horses,” “In Order of Disappearance,” “A Somewhat Gentle Man” and “Zero Kelvin.” His films have competed for the Golden Bear four times, and “Out Stealing Horses” was Norway’s Oscar submission in 2019.

Moland co-wrote the screenplay with Eidsvold. The film was shot by Oskar Dahlsbakken, with an original score by Danish composer Kaspar Kaae. It is produced by Håkon Øverås for 4 ½ Fiction, in co-production with Scanbox.

#726. AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage

Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

#725. Want to live and work on the moon? NASA is hiring.

Ever looked at the moon and thought, man, I'd love to work there? Well, NASA is hiring.

Announced over the weekend, applications are now open for the next batch of astronauts who will train specifically to work and live on the lunar surface.

The U.S. space agency is looking for the next class to be trained at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, those "who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars." Applications close 11:59 p.m. ET Dec. 3 and NASA will make its selections in late 2027.

Saturday's announcement came with a "NASA wants you" recruitment video, featuring NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Andre Douglas, Deniz Burnham, Randy Bresnik, Kayla Barron, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams.

Notably, remote work isn't available for astronauts, and relocation fees to Houston may be covered by NASA. But the salary is out of this world: between $164,395 to $164,395 per year.

Of course, you can't just spacewalk into a job on the moon. To apply, you'll need to be a U.S. citizen with a master's degree in a STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) field from an accredited institution. If you don't have the latter, NASA will also accept currently enrolled or completed Test Pilot School students (who also have a STEM bachelor's degree), people with medical degrees with professional experience or completed residency training, or people who have completed two years of a STEM-based doctoral program. Candidates also need at least three post-degree years in their field.

Applying pilots also need to have considerable flight experience and pilot-in-command time whether in high-performance jet, rotary-wing, or other fix-wing aircrafts.

Along with a dazzling CV, applicants will need to upload five references (not letters of recommendation), all STEM-related academic transcripts, and if necessary, a completed pilot qualifications form. Candidates can then track their applications online.

It's been two years since NASA opened astronaut applications in 2024, from which 10 candidates made it through from over 8,000 applications. Nicknamed "The Platypi," the class of 2026 are currently training at Johnson Space Center. When their training's complete, they'll join the 32 active astronauts at NASA in missions and tasks like spacecraft development and maintenance (including those all-important spacewalks), research experiments, Mission Control ground support, and more. Who knows? A future Artemis mission could be on your CV.

"This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a press statement. "The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars."

So, if you think you meet NASA's requirements (and I certainly don't), you can apply to be an astronaut via the U.S. government's job website.

"The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes. We've now cracked it open a little farther."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ever since NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) started observing the early universe, it has been providing almost as many surprises as it has answers. One such surprise are the so-called Little Red Dots, cosmic objects that seemingly disappear completely before the universe is two billion years old.

New research suggests that Little Red Dots may actually be connected primordial black holes, tiny black holes born not from dying stars but rather from fluctuations in the density of matter just after the Big Bang, in the earliest moments of cosmic history. Should they exist, primordial black holes would predate stars, galactic dust particles, and elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Now, researchers have used JWST data to test whether one particular Little Red Dot, known as blackAbell 2744-QSO1 (QSO1), could host a primordial black hole.

"A black hole is an object born from the gravitational death of a star. Primordial black holes are a very different story," study team member Valerio De Luca, of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) in Maryland, said in a statement.

"They come from the physics of the early universe that predates the first stars, when the universe was expanding exponentially in time and space. So the mechanisms for creating primordial black holes are different," De Luca added.

Though scientists have theorized about the existence of primordial black holes since they were first proposed by Stephen Hawking in the 1970s, no hard evidence has presented itself. One of the issues scientists have puzzled over is how to tell the difference between a primordial black hole and a "traditional" or astrophysical black hole formed from the supernova death and collapse of a massive star.

"Little Red Dots could surround astrophysical black holes, and most probably many of them do, but they could also be primordial black holes, if primordial black holes exist," De Luca said. "So the question becomes, Which ones are primordial and how can we tell?"

De Luca and colleagues turned their attention to QS01, located around 13.1 billion light-years from Earth, which is seen as it was just 700 million years after the Big Bang. What makes this Little Red Dot stand out is the fact that it is almost entirely composed of hydrogen and helium. Because these were the universe's first elements, it could be more unspoiled and primordial than other Little Red Dots.

The team modeled how a Little Red Dot like QS01 could form from a primordial black hole. That was necessary because the circumstances under which this could happen would have to be very specific.

"There are constraints on primordial black holes from cosmological observations," said team member Loris Del Grosso, also of JHU's Department of Physics and Astronomy. "There can only be so many primordial black holes in the universe, for example, and there cannot be too many of them in a given cluster."

Considering three possible scenarios, the team found that the most likely situation is a smaller primordial black hole consuming surrounding gas and energy until it grew to be the size of QSO1.

"The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes," Del Grosso said. "We've now cracked it open a little farther by showing some scenarios are more likely than others."

Del Grosso and crew now intend to look at the other 100 or so Little Red Dots seen by the JWST to determine how many of them could have started life as primordial black holes.

Then scientists may finally have the evidence to say these long-theorized ancient black holes actually existed.

"We don't have a clear understanding of what happens in the early universe right after the Big Bang," De Luca concluded. "If primordial black holes do exist, then something had to happen to make them in the first place, which would be a groundbreaking discovery in physics."

The team's findings were published in June in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #722. MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures

Scientists have spent decades trying to control how tiny particles connect to form advanced materials. Now, researchers at MIT and their collaborators have discovered that doing the exact opposite of what was previously believed necessary can produce remarkable results.

Instead of relying on rigid molecular connections to hold nanoparticles in carefully planned arrangements, the team developed extremely flexible connectors that bend and adjust as particles come together. This unexpected strategy gives scientists a new way to control how nanoparticles organize themselves, allowing them to create crystal structures that have never been observed before.

The discovery could help overcome a major obstacle in materials science and open new possibilities for creating substances with precisely engineered properties. Potential applications include electronics, medicine, energy technologies, agriculture, and chemical manufacturing.

The findings, described in a paper that will appear in Nature Materials, demonstrate how the flexibility and electrical charges of molecular connectors can determine the structures that nanoparticles form.

MIT Researchers Challenge 20 Years of Materials Science

"People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into," says Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. "This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn't been investigated before. It's exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It's the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well."

The research team also included MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi, University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger, MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa, Matthew Ye PhD '26, and Arthi Jayaraman, a former professor at the University of Delaware.

At the heart of the discovery is a basic principle of materials science: The way a material's smallest components are arranged determines how that material behaves.

"That means if you know what your building blocks are and how they're arranged, you can explain what properties materials have," Macfarlane says. "Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties."

This principle is especially important when working with nanoparticles, which are extremely small pieces of matter whose shapes, sizes, and properties can be adjusted for different purposes. Scientists already use individual nanoparticles in technologies involving drug delivery, energy storage, computing, and sensors.

But turning these tiny building blocks into larger, organized materials presents a difficult challenge.

Why Nanoparticles Are So Difficult to Control

One of the biggest obstacles is controlling how nanoparticles attach to one another. Scientists need to determine not only how many neighboring particles each nanoparticle connects with, but also the directions in which those connections form.

Without that control, nanoparticles tend to assemble into tightly packed arrangements that restrict the variety of structures researchers can produce. This limits their ability to create materials with unusual or specialized properties.

Researchers have traditionally approached the problem in two ways. One strategy involves changing the shapes of nanoparticles to influence how they fit together. Another involves modifying specific areas of their surfaces so that only certain regions attract neighboring particles.

In effect, scientists attempt to control where the particles stick to one another, much like designing puzzle pieces that can connect only in particular positions.

Although these methods can produce useful structures, they are often complicated, highly specialized, and difficult to adapt for large-scale production.

"The challenge with both of those approaches is they're difficult to do synthetically as we make the particles," Macfarlane explains. "The methods for defining stickiness that have been developed are always bespoke: They work for one material, at one size scale, in one condition. It's good for studying, but you can't do much with it."

Both strategies also depend on molecular connectors called ligands. These molecules attach to the surfaces of nanoparticles and help link neighboring particles together.

Traditionally, researchers have tried to make these ligands rigid so the connections remain at carefully controlled angles. This helps maintain a desired arrangement, but it also restricts the types of structures that can form and the functions they can perform.

The MIT team decided to explore a radically different possibility.

A Surprising Discovery About Flexible Molecular Bonds

Rather than forcing molecular connectors to remain in fixed positions, the researchers wondered whether giving them almost complete freedom to bend could offer an entirely new form of control.

"We thought, 'Let's do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn't matter what direction they're initially pointing.' The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind," Macfarlane says.

The idea reverses the usual approach to nanoparticle assembly. Instead of controlling the orientation of every connection in advance, the scientists allow the connectors to adjust naturally as the particles interact.

Macfarlane's laboratory has spent years developing ways to construct different types of nanoparticles using attached polymer chains. Polymers are large molecules made of repeating smaller units, and their flexibility makes them useful for creating adjustable molecular connections.

For the new system, the team equipped nanoparticles with highly flexible ligands that carry electrical charges at their ends. Some have positive charges, while others have negative charges.

Because opposite electrical charges attract, the connector molecules naturally bend toward partners with the opposite charge. This attraction helps the nanoparticles join together, while the flexibility of the connectors influences how many connections each particle can make.

"The idea is, instead of defining a specific direction the bonds are going to occur in with complicated synthesis methods, we just said, 'The bonds are going to be as flexible as they want to be, and they'll spontaneously go to whatever valency is going to maximize bond stability,'" Macfarlane says.

In this context, valency refers to the number of connections a nanoparticle forms with its neighbors. By allowing the connectors to move freely, the researchers found that the system could naturally settle into stable arrangements without requiring every connection to be designed beforehand.

Scientists Create Crystal Structures Never Seen Before

Experiments led by Sbalbi demonstrated that the researchers could adjust the connections between nanoparticles by changing two relatively straightforward characteristics: the sizes of the particles and the lengths of their flexible molecular chains.

These adjustments altered how the particles assembled, giving the team control over the number of neighboring particles each one could connect with.

Most importantly, the researchers used this method to produce previously unseen crystal structures.

Crystals are materials whose building blocks form organized, repeating patterns. In this case, the repeating arrangements are made from nanoparticles rather than individual atoms or small molecules. Such ordered nanoparticle networks are often called superlattices.

By reducing the number of connections between neighboring particles, the team was able to create more open arrangements instead of the densely packed structures that commonly form during nanoparticle assembly.

"Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has," Macfarlane explains. "The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before."

The results suggest that molecular flexibility, once viewed as an obstacle to precise nanoparticle assembly, can instead become a powerful tool for engineering new material structures.

A New Path Toward Customizable Designer Materials

The researchers believe their method could bring scientists closer to a long-sought goal in materials science: choosing the properties of individual nanoparticles independently of the larger structures into which they assemble.

Ideally, scientists could select nanoparticles for their electrical, optical, chemical, or other useful characteristics and then organize those particles into whatever arrangement best serves a particular application.

In practice, however, existing assembly methods have made that level of flexibility difficult to achieve.

"We in the nanoparticle assembly community talk about having completely independent control over what your particle is and what assembly it goes into," Macfarlane says. "In theory, that should be the case. In reality, it absolutely has not been."

The new approach could help close that gap. Because the researchers can influence nanoparticle arrangements through the flexibility of their connectors and the attraction between electrical charges, they may be able to create a wider variety of structures without the complicated manufacturing techniques required by traditional methods.

The team also sees the discovery as a promising route toward producing customizable materials at larger scales, potentially helping move nanoparticle technologies beyond laboratory experiments and into practical use.

Potential Applications in Electronics, Medicine, and Energy

The ability to build more open and varied nanoparticle structures could prove particularly valuable for developing advanced materials.

In photonics, which involves controlling and manipulating light, precisely organized nanoparticles could help researchers engineer materials with specialized optical properties. In chemical catalysis, where substances accelerate chemical reactions, new particle arrangements could create opportunities to improve the way catalysts operate.

The approach may also support future developments in medicine, agriculture, electronics, and energy technologies.

A major advantage is that nanoparticles can already possess a wide range of desirable properties. By controlling how those particles come together, scientists may be able to combine their individual capabilities in new ways.

"Nanoparticle superlattices offer a way to create designer materials where your building blocks have all sort sorts of unique properties," Macfarlane says. "But just densely packing these nanoparticles together limits your applications. This offers a way to get less dense formations of nanoparticles, and that's where a lot of the interesting applications are."

Although further development will be needed to translate the method into commercial technologies, the discovery establishes molecular flexibility as a new strategy for creating materials with tailored structures.

Instead of treating bending molecular connections as a problem to eliminate, scientists may now be able to use that flexibility to unlock arrangements that rigid designs could not easily achieve.

The research received partial support from the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy.
