#684. A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

For some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms.

The molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an important role in how cells generate energy. In a small clinical trial, breast cancer survivors who took the supplement for eight weeks reported noticeable improvements in thinking, memory, concentration, and fatigue.

The results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how quickly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility. Although larger studies are needed to confirm the findings, the results suggest a potentially new way to address a problem that has long been difficult to treat.

"Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person's daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it," said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study's first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Why Brain Fog Can Persist After Cancer Treatment

Cognitive difficulties are a lasting concern for many people who survive breast cancer. Researchers estimate that roughly 15% to 25% experience ongoing problems with memory, concentration, or other thinking abilities after their diagnosis and treatment. These symptoms are often described as "chemo brain" or "brain fog."

Despite the name, chemotherapy is not necessarily the only cause. Scientists increasingly recognize that cancer-related cognitive impairment can develop through several overlapping processes. The cancer itself, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral influences may all contribute.

Because the causes are complicated and effective treatments remain limited, researchers are investigating ways to address the underlying changes that may disrupt normal brain function.

One area of interest involves the relationship between inflammation, brain chemistry, and energy production. Inflammation linked to cancer and its treatments may interfere with glutamate signaling, an important part of communication between nerve cells. It may also disturb the processes that allow brain cells to produce and use energy efficiently. Together, these disruptions could contribute to difficulties with thinking and persistent mental exhaustion.

Oxaloacetate attracted the UCLA team's attention because it participates in both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate. The researchers wanted to learn whether providing additional oxaloacetate through a supplement might reduce the cognitive symptoms and fatigue experienced by cancer survivors.

Testing Oxaloacetate for Brain Fog and Fatigue

To investigate, the researchers carried out a phase II clinical trial involving 18 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer between one and five years earlier. All participants were experiencing substantial cognitive difficulties when they entered the study.

The women were approximately 50 years old on average. Most had undergone chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were still receiving endocrine therapy during the trial.

Each participant was instructed to take 500 milligrams of oxaloacetate twice a day for eight weeks. The researchers tracked changes in cognitive symptoms using questionnaires completed by the participants, along with standardized tests designed to evaluate memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function. Executive function includes the mental abilities needed to organize activities, maintain focus, make plans, and manage tasks.

The study also examined fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical health, and mental well-being. Throughout the treatment period, the team monitored participants for possible side effects.

Brain Fog Scores Improved After Eight Weeks

Of the 18 women enrolled, 16 completed the full eight weeks of supplementation. Every participant who finished the treatment reported significant improvement in her cognitive symptoms.

The changes were particularly striking on the study's main measure of perceived cognitive impairment. Before treatment, the participants had an average score of 29.1. After eight weeks, that average had climbed to 55.5, placing the group in the range considered normal rather than impaired.

Signs of improvement were already apparent after four weeks, and the benefits reported by participants generally became more pronounced as treatment continued.

The results extended beyond memory and concentration. Participants reported significantly less fatigue, including the mental exhaustion that can make everyday activities difficult. They also described meaningful improvements in their ability to function physically.

Standardized cognitive testing provided additional encouraging evidence. Researchers observed improvements in processing speed and executive function, suggesting that some aspects of thinking performance may have improved alongside the participants' perceptions of their symptoms.

However, the scientists emphasized that these results remain preliminary because the trial included so few participants.

Promising Results, but More Research Is Needed

Oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated during the eight-week study. The most frequently reported side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea.

Two women stopped taking the supplement because of gastrointestinal symptoms. No serious adverse events were recorded.

Despite the encouraging improvements, the researchers cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about the supplement's effectiveness. The trial was small and did not include a placebo group or another comparison group. Without that comparison, it is not possible to determine whether oxaloacetate itself caused the improvements.

"These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment," Ganz said.

Larger Clinical Trial Will Test the Supplement's Benefits

To build on these initial findings, the UCLA team has been preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial involving breast cancer survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment. The study was expected to begin enrolling participants in late 2026.

By comparing oxaloacetate with a placebo, the researchers hope to establish whether the supplement produces measurable benefits beyond those that might occur without active treatment.

The investigators are also conducting preclinical research in mice to better understand how oxaloacetate affects the body and brain. These experiments include a placebo-controlled study examining whether the molecule produces similar improvements (improved fatigue and physical function) in animals.

The research received partial financial support from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

In addition to Ganz, the study's authors were Kathleen Van Dyk, PhD, Catherine M. Crespi, PhD, Laura Petersen, MS, Mina Sedrak, MD, MS, and Julienne Bower, PhD, all affiliated with UCLA.

As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes, ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon, just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look.

Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30, the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras.

It has a 1.2-inch (30 mm) aperture, two 3.7 MP cameras and four-element apochromatic optics bundled into a compact build.

Both produce 1,440 x 2,560-pixel images, while a much-improved 43.5-degree wide-angle camera can capture the Milky Way, constellations, star trails and nightscapes. Built-in filters, a mosaic mode and equatorial (EQ) tracking add considerable deep-sky astrophotography potential.

For a telescope weighing just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg), it’s impressive. It easily fits into a camera bag and could happily live on a bookshelf.

I’ve already photographed the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Pleiades (M45), the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) and the North America Nebula (NGC 7000). The results are excellent for such a small instrument, especially when imaging nebulas with its built-in dual-band filter, which helps reduce light pollution.

The Seestar app adds new in-app post-processing options, so you don’t have to mess around with any of that — though you can also export everything as lossless FITS files. The S30 Plus also includes a magnetic solar filter, enabling you to indulge in solar photography safely.

With Dwarflab’s $1,299 Draco (3.5-inch/90mm aperture) recently landed in stores and Vaonis’ own $4,990 Atlas (3.1-inch/80mm aperture) not available until 2027, ZWO’s decision to offer an upgraded entry-level smart telescope that buyers can get their hands on right now looks particularly smart.

With ZWO's pattern of delivering cheaper smart telescopes without sacrificing on quality, the Seestar S30 Plus could be one of Christmas 2026’s best gifts for anyone interested in astronomy — and maybe that’s the point of it. Either way, first impressions are good. A full review is coming tomorrow, so check back at Space.com to find out our full thoughts and testing.

#680. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

#679. GTA 6 preload release date: When you can download the game

For anyone who has already pre-ordered Grand Theft Auto VI, it's about to take up a huge amount of space on your console's hard drive in the very near future.

That's because it's almost time to preload the most anticipated game of the year. If you don't normally engage with games this way, it means that anyone who has purchased GTA 6 will be able to install the full game on their hard drive before release. According to Rockstar, preloading will work slightly differently on PS5 and Xbox consoles. For PS5 owners, preloading will begin on Tuesday, Nov. 10 at midnight local time wherever you are. For Xbox players, preloading starts at 12 a.m. GMT on Tuesday and runs simultaneously for everyone.

To be clear, preloading the game early does not mean you can play it early, unless you set your console to New Zealand time. It will be locked and unplayable until it's officially out in your region.

Rockstar also confirmed in that post that the game will take up to 212GB of space on your hard drive, so start deleting games right now if you need to.

#678. Welcome to Weed Island

Steven Tan walks along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones.

But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.”

Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification.

Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy.

Jersey, a British Crown Dependency that sits between the UK and France, that has become an integral hub for the medical cannabis industry.

Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”

Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says.

The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing.

Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says.

Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich.

Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor.

Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO. That year, it was valued at just £3.7 million, despite having spent as much as £30 million on its weed-growing facility.

Tan nevertheless saw a lot of potential, and over the last two years has seen capacity at the site increase from 25 percent to 75 percent. He believes the £8.4 million of product the company exported last year is just the beginning.

Northern Leaf's 100,000-square-foot growing facility. “On 20 percent of the land,” says CEO Steven Tan, “I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.”

Sarah Clover, a barrister at Kings Chambers who works on cannabis licensing in Jersey, told WIRED the island’s advantage is hard to replicate. Growers are inspected by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is known for enforcing rigorous standards on quality. “Anybody buying from Jersey knows that the stuff coming out of it is absolutely gold standard, because the MHRA says it is,” she says. Permits, however, are handled by a small team on the island: “You can make an application for a permit on a Monday and get it on a Tuesday.”

Many within the Jersey medicinal cannabis industry now want to go beyond growing the raw ingredient and package it for export as a final product on the island. Northern Leaf already has the facilities to do so, but Jersey law dictates it can only export bulk amounts of raw cannabis for other companies to process and pack for distribution and sale. The company is waiting to see if Jersey will change its law. “At the minute we’re kind of on this seesaw—which way will the island go?” Clover says. “It could really take off here. Jersey could be a life sciences hub, not just for cannabis but for all sorts of pharmaceuticals.”

But running a cannabis business on a small island poses challenges, and not everyone is enthused about the idea of expansion. Tan has faced off against residents every time that the facility has expanded production. Some locals have complained that they can smell cannabis from their balconies. Others have linked the growing industry to concerns over misuse of cannabis on the island, despite the fact that all of its product is exported. Cannabis is a “contributory factor” in 22 percent of admissions to the island’s acute mental health ward, according to Jersey’s health minister.

One patient, Michael, told WIRED that he was prescribed medical cannabis for 18 months after having tried two other prescribed medications for insomnia and anxiety. “The initial assessment was simple. I had a meeting with the cannabis doctor who was pretty evangelical about its medicinal properties. They check your medical history with your GP, and within 10 days you’re good to go,” he says.

Michael was prescribed 30 grams a month of “unbelievably good” cannabis and told that if he ran out he could back and ask for more. “I stopped because it was seriously affecting my mental health [and] I have since seen a psychiatric professional who said I should never have been prescribed it given my documented mental health history,” he says.

Illegal resale of medical cannabis is also an issue, with a rise in so-called “user-dealers,” who sell their excess medical marijuana to others. Jersey Police told WIRED this “undermines the legal framework and creates opportunities for criminal supply.”

Overall, however, cannabis-related offenses have dropped since Jersey legalized medical cannabis in 2019—from 216 in 2016 to just 12, as of July 2026.

Tan is circumspect about the challenges of operating on Jersey. “Culturally, the people here are harder to convince about cannabis,” he says. “It’s an older society.” But after 25 years working in the industry, he’s used to the pushback.

“It’s a normal challenge,” he says. “And I think when anyone sits down and meets me, they understand. This isn’t a bunch of stoners growing a bit of weed in a plastic greenhouse.”

While Jersey’s medical cannabis industry grows, some people on the island want to go further. In 2024, a vote to decriminalize recreational cannabis was defeated by a single vote in the island’s parliament. When it was brought back for another vote by the island’s then health minister, it was withdrawn before it could be debated. It is expected to be brought back before the parliament in the coming months.

Some individuals on the island have decided not to wait. By exploiting a loophole in current laws, they have made Jersey one of the only places in Europe outside of Amsterdam where THC products can be purchased and consumed legally.

One morning in February 2024, Gary Tucker arrived at work, his weed shop in St Helier, Jersey, to find a dozen customs officers and the local media waiting outside. It was a raid—and not his first. The officers emptied shelves and boxes into bin bags. “They were literally running their arms down the shelves and putting everything into bags. They took everything,” Tucker, a California native and former analyst in the US Army, told WIRED.

Tucker operates outside of Jersey’s medical cannabis industry. His shop, Bailiwick Botanicals, sells products that are clearly recreational: hash cakes, gummies, and other snacks, all infused with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis that gets you high and is heavily controlled.

He’s able to do this owing to a loophole in Jersey law which allows the sale of products containing CBD—another critical ingredient in cannabis, but one that doesn’t get you high. Jersey’s law says that the amount of THC in CBD products cannot exceed 3 percent of the weight of the CBD. So, if you want to sell products with high levels of THC, you just have to boost the CBD. “It’s just a math equation,” Tucker says.

Tucker admits it isn’t an ideal situation: studies suggest that ingesting high levels of CBD can cause liver damage. But he sees that as an issue with the regulation, not his solution. “I’m just following consumer demand,” he says.

Tucker is somewhat evangelical about the properties of cannabis. In his time as a weapons trainer for the military, he struggled with the mental health impacts of hearing that recruits he had trained had been killed in action. “I needed to step back from it. It started to really affect my mind,” Tucker says.

Veterans he knew were turning to cannabis, and Tucker began buying it on the black market. “It was the only thing that helped me,” he says. ”Cannabis gave me my life back.”

Tucker currently manufactures most of his products in the US before shipping them to Sark—a smaller Channel Island best known for having no cars and also its own government—and then to Jersey. New regulations in the US, however, mean Tucker may need to change his approach.

Tucker sees Jersey as a potential export hub for THC products to Europe. He believes Jersey’s budding weed industry should push beyond medical cannabis and into the recreational market. “This isn’t just a bunch of guys in a cellar somewhere. Not only does cannabis help people, but getting it to the shelf creates jobs. From the grower to the retailer. It permeates across all industries. We’re making cosmetics. We’re making gummies. We’re making drinks,” he says.

After the 2024 raid, Bailiwick Botanicals shut its doors for two weeks, and its full stock wasn’t returned until six months later. As of June 2026, Tucker and his team are selling THC-infused fudge, chocolate, and other sweets. His newest product, THC-infused coffee beans, is selling well. The police have stayed away.

In a written statement to WIRED, Jersey’s government said that the “possibility of abuse of our limits to get round the law in other jurisdictions is a matter of concern to the Government of Jersey and we are looking at ways to address it. Work is underway to consider whether Jersey’s existing legal exemptions for CBD products require amendment.”

“These plants are all different. Just like humans," says Tan.

For his part, Tan is reluctant to be drawn on his views on the so-called “rec” (recreational) market. For now, Jersey still has harsh sentencing rules on recreational cannabis use, with the penalties for possession and possession with intent to supply remaining up to five years and 14 years in jail, respectively. The proposed (and withdrawn) law to decriminalize cannabis notes that, the way the law is currently written, someone who rolled three joints and gave one to a friend would be guilty of supply and receive a criminal record. “Without change, people will continue receiving serious criminal records for small amounts … punishments [that] can result in additional harms greater than the drug itself,” it said.

While Jersey makes its own laws, however, it may not be able to completely legalize cannabis. Jersey is a signatory to the UN Convention on drugs control via the UK, and the UK Home Office would undoubtedly have a view if the island were to set itself up as an “Amsterdam on the Sea.” In 2022, an effort by the government of Bermuda (a British Overseas Territory) to legalize recreational cannabis was blocked after the UK withheld Royal Assent from the bill.

Back at the Northern Leaf warehouse in the Jersey parish of St Lawrence, Tan is flipping the lids off large boxes and rifling through clear plastic bags packed full of cannabis.

This is all weed that will not be sold, either because there were issues with production or the THC levels were too low. Instead, it is taken to a secure area of the facility where it is locked away in a reinforced armored vault. Specialist staff with bodycams take the bags to the island’s incinerator, where it is unceremoniously burned, as required by law.

Tan regularly makes a case to the government for changes to the law and support for the cannabis industry, such as an industrial energy tariff to help with spiraling energy costs.

He has claimed that Jersey could be home to “the Monsanto of cannabis,” alluding to the agricultural giant that was acquired by pharmaceutical company Bayer in 2018 for $66 billion. He’d like to get deeper into the genetics of cannabis, form a tissue-culture lab, and “bring out strains that nobody has ever seen.”

But speaking of himself, he references a different genre of business: He’s Willy Wonka, but for weed. Thirty years ago, when Tan quit corporate finance, his father warned him that he could make a lot more money if he stayed in banking. “And you know what, he was right,” he says. “But I would not have had nearly as much fun.”

#677. Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered

A tiny fish with brilliant orange markings has been discovered in the Brazilian Amazon, but scientists warn that the newly identified species may already be at risk of extinction. Found in a handful of forest pools threatened by human activity, the colorful fish has prompted researchers to call for urgent conservation measures.

The new species, named Laimosemion laranja, belongs to a group of small freshwater fish known as killifish. It measures less than three centimeters in standard length, but its appearance is anything but ordinary. Males have rows of bright orange spots along the front half of their bodies, followed by bold orange chevron patterns near the tail. These vivid markings stand out against their pale gray sides.

The discovery was made during fieldwork in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá, a state in northern Brazil. The research team included scientists from the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte, Instituto Peixe das Nuvens, Universidade Federal do Pará, and University of West Florida.

A Striking Discovery in the Amazon Rainforest

The researchers were exploring how different freshwater fish in the Rivulidae family have evolved their life cycles and survival strategies across Brazil's diverse environments. During their surveys, they encountered a fish whose unusual coloration immediately stood out.

"We are developing a research project aimed at investigating the evolution of life-history strategies in freshwater fishes of the family Rivulidae across different biomes in Brazil," said lead researcher Yuri Abrantes of the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. "During our sampling in small rivers locally known as 'igarapés' in the Rio Cajari region, in Amapá State, we found this fish with a very striking coloration, which immediately caught our attention."

Although the fish looked different from known species, its appearance alone was not enough to establish that it was new to science. The team carefully examined its body proportions, counted its scales, and studied features of its skeleton. They compared these characteristics with those of closely related species and analyzed its mitochondrial DNA to determine whether it represented a distinct species.

"It was an unexpected moment," Abrantes recalled. "Initially, what most caught our attention was the impressive coloration of the males and females, which was unlike anything we had previously encountered in the study area. This sparked our admiration and a great deal of curiosity."

Genetic testing ultimately confirmed that the fish was a previously unrecognized species. For the researchers, the finding was particularly meaningful because it highlighted how much remains to be discovered in parts of the Amazon that are both poorly studied and increasingly threatened.

Once the genetic analysis confirmed the fish's distinct identity, he said, "it was something special, as we saw an opportunity to contribute to increasing our knowledge of Amazonian biodiversity and to draw attention to the conservation of areas that are still poorly explored but highly threatened."

Why Scientists Named the New Fish Laranja

The name Laimosemion laranja reflects both the fish's remarkable appearance and the place where it was discovered. In Portuguese, laranja means orange, referring to both the color and the fruit. The name also pays tribute to Laranjal do Jari, the municipality in Amapá where the species was found.

"We wanted to choose a name that would highlight a characteristic of the fish while also fostering a sense of connection with the people of the region where it was discovered," Abrantes explained.

Beyond its colorful appearance, the discovery could help scientists better understand the evolution of Amazonian killifish. Some members of this group have developed an extraordinary way to survive in habitats that periodically dry out. Their embryos can stop developing and remain dormant in damp mud, resuming development when seasonal rains refill the pools.

"Laimosemion represents one of the five independent origins of the annual life cycle within the family Rivulidae," said Abrantes. "Laimosemion laranja is particularly interesting because it expands our knowledge of the diversity and evolution of this group in the region."

Newly Discovered Amazon Fish May Already Be Endangered

Despite the excitement surrounding the discovery, the future of Laimosemion laranja is uncertain. Scientists have found it in only three small forest pools near Laranjal do Jari, and every known location shows signs of environmental disturbance.

Deforestation, mining, and urban development are putting pressure on the surrounding habitats. One of the pools is close to water that has been discolored by sediment from mining activities. Another is located within the city itself, where plastic pollution is affecting the environment.

The species' entire known range is estimated to cover just 25 square kilometers. Because its habitat is so restricted and faces multiple threats, the researchers believe the fish meets the criteria for classification as Endangered under guidelines established by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

To improve its chances of survival, the team has recommended expanding the boundaries of the nearby Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to include the areas where the fish lives.

The discovery adds another species to the Amazon's remarkable biological diversity while underscoring the need to protect habitats that scientists have barely begun to explore. Without stronger conservation measures, species such as Laimosemion laranja could face serious threats before researchers have the opportunity to fully understand them.

The study was published in the open access journal Zoosystematics and Evolution.

#676. Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a new understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved.

The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land.

Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned.

Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans.

"After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," said Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare."

A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue

The remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis, an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented.

Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual.

"Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found."

The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared.

"It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur."

Ancient Feeding Structures Reveal Evolutionary Secrets

The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings.

Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents.

The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist.

"Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed."

Researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years.

"Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us new insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years."

A Rare Window Into Earth's Earliest Ocean Ecosystems

Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era.

The Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited.

Crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives.

"Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright said.

"By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere."

The biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another.

Because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life.

An Extraordinary Discovery Hidden in a Museum Collection

Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found.

Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums.

Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most important features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked.

"New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright said. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries."

The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations.

Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely.

Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence.

"This discovery highlights the importance of museum collections and the community support that keeps them alive," Cole said. "Without the dedication of many people caring for these collections, this research would never have been possible."

More Discoveries May Be Waiting in Museum Drawers

The finding also demonstrates why preserving and maintaining fossil collections is essential for future research.

At the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Cole and Wright oversee invertebrate paleontology collections containing more than one million specimens. Additional fossils are added every year, creating new opportunities to investigate ancient organisms and identify previously unrecognized species.

With collections of this size, no individual researcher could possibly examine every specimen in detail. A fossil that appears ordinary today might become the focus of a major discovery when studied by someone with a different specialty or new scientific tools.

Making collections available to researchers around the world increases the chances that these overlooked treasures will eventually receive the attention they deserve.

"This is why we work to make our collections accessible to researchers around the world," Wright said. "There are simply too many fossils to study over one person's career. There's more than a lifetime's worth of discoveries waiting to be found."

The extraordinary crinoid fossil is a reminder that some of the most revealing clues about Earth's distant past may already have been collected. They are simply waiting for someone to recognize what makes them special.

#675. Bikers and Bug-Lovers Join Forces to Fight a New Google Data Center

On Wednesday afternoon, Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London.

Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site.

Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility.

Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them, hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US, people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works.

Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour. Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week. In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner.

“There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.”

The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake.

Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.)

The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget.

“We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.”

Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030. Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.”

Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.”

There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London.

Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step.

“These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”

NASA's Curiosity Mars rover is sizing up its next dig site on the Red Planet.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of the Mars site, informally named "Nazca," as thoroughly as possible before drilling into it.

Curiosity snapped the close-up image on Oct. 18, 2026, using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). The image shows multiple roughly disk-shaped potential crystal formations at the rover's next drill target.

MAHLI is located on the turret at the end of the rover's robotic arm. It uses an onboard focusing process to make a composite of images of the same target acquired at different positions to focus on multiple features in a single image.

Scientists theorize that the "discs and needles" texture takes its characteristic shape as crystals, or "crystal forms," grow.

The relatively large sizes of the crystal forms at "Nazca" may provide clues about the temperatures at which they grew, as well as information about the abundance of salts and fluids in the area at the time. Complicating this picture, however, is the fact that mineral crystals can be replaced by other minerals after their original crystallization. The new minerals are known as "pseudomorphs," because they have the same shape as the original minerals but not the same composition or molecular structure.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of Nazca — which shares its name with an ancient South American civilization that's famous for the large designs it etched into the rock and dirt — before drilling begins. The NASA researchers will then be able to compare the deeper composition to the surface-level composition.

#673. A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid

Scientists have demonstrated an extraordinary form of quantum matter that combines two properties that seem incompatible. Known as a supersolid, this unusual state has the orderly structure of a crystal while also displaying the frictionless flow associated with a special kind of liquid. Even more remarkably, researchers have now observed this behavior at room temperature, eliminating the need for the extreme cooling traditionally used to investigate such phenomena.

The breakthrough was achieved by an international team from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). Rather than relying on atoms cooled to temperatures near absolute zero, the scientists created a supersolid using particles that combine properties of light and matter.

Published in Science Advances, the findings introduce a new way to investigate exotic quantum behavior under much more accessible conditions. They could also help advance future technologies ranging from optical computing to highly sensitive sensors.

How Can Matter Behave Like Both a Solid and a Liquid?

Under ordinary circumstances, solids and liquids behave very differently. Crystals have an organized internal structure, with their particles arranged in repeating patterns. Liquids, by comparison, can flow and change shape.

Quantum physics, however, allows matter to behave in ways that would be impossible under the familiar rules of everyday life.

One example is superfluidity, a remarkable phenomenon in which a fluid loses its viscosity, or internal resistance to flowing. A superfluid can move through extremely narrow passages without experiencing the usual friction. Imagine placing an oar into such a liquid. You would encounter almost no resistance until the oar reached a certain speed. Beyond that threshold, tiny swirling structures known as quantum vortices would suddenly form.

During the 1960s, physicists proposed an even stranger possibility. What if a superfluid could also develop the repeating internal structure normally associated with a crystal?

This hypothetical combination became known as a supersolid. In such a state, the material exhibits the spatial organization of a solid while retaining the remarkable flow properties of a superfluid.

For decades, supersolidity remained a theoretical concept. Experimental confirmation finally arrived in 2017, when researchers observed the phenomenon in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. These condensates form when particles enter a collective quantum state and begin behaving as a coordinated system rather than as separate individuals.

The catch was that producing these conditions generally required sophisticated equipment capable of cooling matter to temperatures extremely close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

Creating a Quantum Supersolid Using Light Instead of Cold Atoms

The international TopoLight consortium approached the challenge from a different direction. Instead of using ultracold atoms, the researchers worked with unusual hybrid particles called exciton polaritons.

These quasiparticles arise when light interacts so strongly with matter that the two become coupled inside a tiny optical chamber called a microcavity. The resulting particles display characteristics of both light and matter.

Exciton polaritons are extremely short-lived, typically surviving for only a few picoseconds. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. Despite their brief existence, these particles can organize into a Bose-Einstein condensate and collectively exhibit the behavior of a quantum superfluid.

To create the necessary conditions, the team constructed an optical microcavity containing a specially engineered liquid crystal and covered it with an organic semiconductor. The arrangement allowed light and matter to interact strongly enough to produce the desired quantum effects without the need for extreme cooling.

"Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C," says Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures.

That temperature is approximately 140°F, far above the freezing conditions normally associated with experiments involving exotic quantum matter.

Strange Patterns of Light Reveal a Supersolid

How can researchers determine whether a collection of particles has entered such an unusual state?

In this experiment, the evidence appeared in the light emitted by the sample. When the system transitioned into the supersolid phase, researchers observed a series of regularly spaced bright fringes.

These patterns indicated that the particle condensate had spontaneously developed a repeating variation in its density. This type of spatial organization is a defining feature of crystalline structures and an important sign of supersolidity.

But the researchers noticed another intriguing effect.

Each time a laser pulse excited the sample, the bright fringes appeared in a different position. Rather than following a single fixed arrangement, the quantum system repeatedly selected among several equally possible configurations.

"This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking," explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). "Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed."

Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when a system that could exist in several equivalent arrangements settles into one particular configuration. In this case, the effect became visible through the changing positions of the light patterns.

The condensate also displayed another unusual characteristic called a persistent spin helix. This refers to a repeating variation in the polarization of the emitted light. Polarization describes the orientation of light's oscillating electric field.

Together, these observations revealed two different forms of order occurring at the same time. One appeared in the intensity of the emitted light, while the other appeared in its polarization.

A Difficult Experiment With Only Hours to Succeed

Achieving these results required overcoming an unexpected practical obstacle.

The organic semiconductor used in the device gradually reacted with the liquid crystal. As a result, the experimental samples had a limited useful lifetime, giving the scientists only a few hours to collect their measurements after assembly.

This restriction made careful preparation essential. The researchers needed to determine exactly which measurements to perform and in what order before beginning each experimental run.

"We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance," recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper's first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. "Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample."

The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich. There, scientists deposited thin layers of the organic semiconductor onto specialized structures designed to manipulate light. These photonic structures had been manufactured at the Military University of Technology.

The semiconductor itself was not new to the researchers. IBM scientists had investigated its quantum properties for years, including its ability to support Bose-Einstein condensation.

"We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material," says Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. "This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity."

Bringing these materials together ultimately made it possible to observe the unusual supersolid behavior at room temperature.

Why Room Temperature Quantum Matter Matters

The significance of the discovery extends beyond demonstrating another unusual phenomenon predicted by quantum physics.

Many experiments involving exotic quantum states depend on costly cryogenic systems designed to maintain temperatures close to absolute zero. These demanding conditions make research more complicated and can create substantial obstacles when scientists attempt to turn laboratory discoveries into useful technologies.

The new results show that certain exotic quantum effects can instead be investigated in photonic devices that operate at ordinary temperatures.

This could create opportunities for future technologies that use light to process information. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, specialized computing accelerators inspired by the way biological brains process information, and advanced optical sensors.

The computing approach, known as neuromorphic computing, seeks to imitate aspects of the brain's information processing to perform certain tasks more efficiently. Light-based systems could eventually provide new ways to accelerate these operations.

The supersolid's exceptional sensitivity to light polarization may also prove useful for developing sensors capable of detecting extremely subtle optical changes.

These applications remain possibilities for future research, but the ability to generate the underlying quantum behavior without extreme cooling represents an important step toward making such technologies more practical.

Electrically Controlled Quantum Matter Opens New Possibilities

One of the most promising features of the experiment is that the optical device can be adjusted using electricity.

The liquid crystal microcavities provide the first electrically tunable platform for studying supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. This means researchers can alter the optical properties of the system by applying an external voltage.

Earlier experimental approaches did not offer this same degree of electrical control.

The ability to adjust the system dynamically gives physicists greater flexibility when investigating how quantum states emerge, interact, and respond to changing conditions.

It could also become valuable when designing practical quantum photonic devices, where precise control over the behavior of light and matter is essential.

By combining room-temperature operation with electrical tunability, the researchers have established a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena that previously required far more demanding experimental conditions.

About the University of Warsaw Faculty of Physics

The University of Warsaw has a long history of research and education in physics and astronomy. Both disciplines became part of the university in 1816, when they were included in the Faculty of Philosophy. The university subsequently established its Astronomical Observatory in 1825.

Today, the Faculty of Physics includes the Institutes of Experimental Physics, Theoretical Physics, and Geophysics, along with the Department of Mathematical Methods in Physics.

Its research encompasses nearly every major area of modern physics, from the behavior of particles at quantum scales to the structure and evolution of the universe.

The faculty employs more than 250 academic teachers and serves approximately 1,350 students and more than 150 doctoral students.

According to Shanghai's Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, the University of Warsaw ranks among the world's top 150 institutions for physics education.

#672. DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office

Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

That, however, has changed. The Trump administration recently argued in court that because the Customs Service’s powers were transferred to DHS following the passing of the Homeland Security Act, it can use that power to tackle its “broad investigative portfolio,” which it says includes enforcing laws “beyond legacy customs and immigration enforcement.”

“When we give law enforcement agencies powerful investigative tools, even with the best intentions and purposes to try to go after legitimate investigations and crime, you have to be really careful,” says Mackey. The newly reported filing is part of an ongoing Freedom of Information Act lawsuit filed by the nonprofit against ICE and DHS.

"The numbers reported to EFF amount to a dragnet domestic surveillance program by Trump's Homeland Security Department,” says US senator Ron Wyden of Oregon.

ICE did not respond to questions about why there’s been such a huge increase compared to prior years, but Mackey speculates that it may be because there is virtually no downside to filing them.

“The worst thing that will happen to ICE is that the service that receives it says it's not going to respond,” says Mackey. If that happens, ICE can just take the company to court to force it to comply, as it recently did with Google, or withdraw it and try to get the information it’s after by issuing a grand jury subpoena, as the Intercept reported it recently did with Reddit.

“Congress desperately needs to pass my bipartisan legislation to drastically curb federal subpoenas, including consequences for officials who abuse surveillance authorities,” says Wyden, referencing his proposed Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act. “Next year, I plan to use the Senate Finance Committee gavel to get to the bottom of HSI's unprecedented misuse of customs law to target Trump's enemies.”

#671. Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.

Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.

"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."

How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.

In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.

A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.

Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.

"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.

"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.

Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.

"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.

The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
